## Goal

By the end you should be able to define a chemical **measurand**, distinguish
concentration from amount, show individual analytical observations, and explain
what a sample comparison supports. Do the small calculations on paper before R.

## Background

A measurand names the intended quantity, material and conditions. Here it is
chloride mass concentration in supplied collected water, in **mg chloride/L**.
The analyte is chloride; the matrix contains water and other species. A measured
signal becomes this quantity only through a suitable chemical measurement model.

For a homogeneous solution, $c=m/V$ and $m=cV$. If no analyte is lost or added,
dilution gives $c_f=c_oV_a/V_f$. Final volume means the **total** after preparation,
including solvent and reagents. The collected material, aliquot and final flask
are different stages; name the stage in a reported concentration.

## By hand

**B1.** The analysis establishes 0.0750 mg chloride in a 25.00 mL portion.
Calculate concentration in mg/L. What information would still be needed to claim
a location-wide mean? [Hint](#hint-b1)

**B2.** A homogeneous solution is 20.0 mg/L. Calculate the analyte amount in
(a) 0.250 L and (b) 0.500 L. Does its concentration change when a larger portion
is taken? [Hint](#hint-b2)

**B3.** A 10.00 mL aliquot is made to 50.00 mL total. The final concentration is
0.800 mg/L. Find the original concentration and analyte amount in the aliquot.
[Hint](#hint-b3)

**B4.** Four inlet samples give 18, 20, 19 and 21 mg/L; four outlet samples give
12, 13, 11 and 14 mg/L. Calculate both means and their difference. State one
supported descriptive claim and one unsupported causal claim. [Hint](#hint-b4)

**B5.** A colleague proposes conductivity as a direct chloride concentration
measurement in a new water matrix. What chemical relation is missing? Would a
perfectly reproducible R report establish it? [Hint](#hint-b5)

## In R

Open the supplied R project and run these commands **from its root**, where
`data/` is located. Keep raw data unchanged. The dataset is simulated and one
row represents one independently collected water sample, not a repeated reading.

```r
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
water <- read_csv("data/course/water.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(water$sample_id), !anyNA(water$chloride_mg_l),
          all(water$collected_l > 0))
summary_water <- water |>
  group_by(location) |>
  summarise(n_samples = n(), mean_mg_l = mean(chloride_mg_l),
            sd_mg_l = sd(chloride_mg_l), .groups = "drop")
summary_water
water <- water |>
  mutate(chloride_g_l = chloride_mg_l / 1000,
         chloride_mg = chloride_mg_l * collected_l)
fig <- ggplot(water, aes(location, chloride_mg_l)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = .08, height = 0, seed = 7)) +
  labs(x = "Sampling location", y = "Chloride (mg/L)") + theme_minimal()
fig
dir.create("output", showWarnings = FALSE)
write_csv(water, "output/water-derived.csv")
ggsave("output/water-observations.png", plot = fig, width = 7, height = 4)
```

**R1.** Check B4 and report both sample counts. Does the row order establish
before/after pairs? [Hint](#hint-r1)

**R2.** Inspect `chloride_g_l` and `chloride_mg`. For W2, explain why the values
are 0.020 g/L and 5.00 mg, with different units and meanings. [Hint](#hint-r2)

**R3.** Write a short result paragraph using the observations and means, then
name the sampling information absent from a location-wide claim. [Hint](#hint-r3)

**R4.** Save the demo export next to the R project, then verify mass conservation.
This guarded block does nothing until that optional file exists:

```r
if (file.exists("concentration-and-amount.csv")) {
  demo <- read_csv("concentration-and-amount.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
  demo <- demo |>
    mutate(recomputed_mg = concentration_mg_l * volume_ml / 1000)
  print(demo)
  stopifnot(all(abs(demo$recomputed_mg - demo$analyte_mg) < 1e-8))
}
```

Which physical failure would make the demo's conservation assumption unsuitable
for a real preparation? [Hint](#hint-r4)

## Hints

::: {#hint-b1 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint B1"}
Convert millilitres to litres before dividing. One portion supplies no sampling
design for an entire location or time period.
:::

::: {#hint-b2 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint B2"}
Use $m=cV$ with litres. The intensive concentration remains fixed when a larger
portion of a homogeneous solution is taken.
:::

::: {#hint-b3 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint B3"}
The preparation factor is final total volume divided by aliquot volume. Calculate
amount either before or after dilution; it should agree.
:::

::: {#hint-b4 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint B4"}
Average each set separately. The observations are from collected waters; they do
not establish a treatment assignment, matching or representative temporal design.
:::

::: {#hint-b5 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint B5"}
Conductivity responds to several mobile ionic species. Reproducing a calculation
does not establish that its chemical model is selective enough.
:::

::: {#hint-explore .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hints E1–E4"}
Track $c$, $V$ and $m$ separately. Changing aliquot volume at fixed dilution
factor changes both original and final volumes proportionally. Adding solvent
at fixed aliquot does not add analyte.
:::

::: {#hint-r1 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint R1"}
[`summarise()`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/summarise.html) returns one
summary per location after `group_by()`. Matching is a design property, not a
coincidence of table positions.
:::

::: {#hint-r2 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint R2"}
Dividing mg/L by 1000 changes to g/L; multiplying mg/L by collected L gives mg.
:::

::: {#hint-r3 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint R3"}
Say what was observed, how many collected samples support it, and which place
and time scope is actually given. Do not invent representativeness.
:::

::: {#hint-r4 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint R4"}
The `/1000` converts mL to L. Consider transfer loss, adsorption, reaction or
analyte in the added solvent.
:::

## Solutions

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions B1–B5"}
**B1.** $0.0750/0.02500=3.00$ mg/L. A location-wide mean also needs a sampling
design defining the location/time population and how portions represent it;
the amount calculation supplies neither that design nor measurement uncertainty.

**B2.** $20.0\times0.250=5.00$ mg and $20.0\times0.500=10.0$ mg. Concentration
is still 20.0 mg/L. Taking more solution changes collected amount, not the
composition of a homogeneous solution.

**B3.** Factor $50.00/10.00=5$; original $0.800\times5=4.00$ mg/L. The aliquot
contains $4.00\times0.01000=0.0400$ mg, equal to $0.800\times0.05000$ mg in
the final flask. “Add 50 mL solvent” would describe a different volume.

**B4.** Inlet mean $(18+20+19+21)/4=19.5$ mg/L; outlet mean
$(12+13+11+14)/4=12.5$ mg/L. Difference 7.0 mg/L. The sampled outlet waters have
a lower observed mean. The data do not establish that a treatment caused this
change, or that every outlet sample at another time would be lower.

**B5.** A justified relation between conductivity and chloride in the proposed
matrix is missing. Other ions can alter conductivity without the same chloride
change. A reproducible wrong model remains wrong; R does not establish selectivity.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions E1–E4"}
**E1.** Original 20 mg/L; original aliquot amount 5 mg; final concentration
10 mg/L in 500 mL. Each statement names a different quantity or stage.

**E2.** A 500 mL aliquot contains 10 mg and becomes 1000 mL at factor 2. Final
concentration remains 10 mg/L because amount and final volume doubled together.

**E3.** At 250 mL and factor 5 the final volume is 1250 mL, final concentration
4 mg/L and amount still 5 mg. $4\times5=20$ mg/L returns to the original basis.
At zero original chloride, amount and final concentration remain zero for every
volume; missing evidence in a real sample would not justify entering zero.

**E4.** `concentration_mg_l` and `volume_ml` change; `analyte_mg` is conserved.
Each row satisfies $m=cV/1000$ when V is in mL. The ideal equality assumes no
chemical or transfer change.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions R1–R4"}
**R1.** Both locations have four collected samples; means match B4. Their sample
SDs are about 1.291 mg/L. No matching variable or paired design is supplied;
row order cannot create pairs.

**R2.** W2 is 20 mg/L, equivalent to 0.020 g/L. Its 0.250 L portion contains
5.00 mg. The first is concentration with a changed mass unit; the second is
amount in a specified portion.

**R3.** One suitable paragraph is: “The four sampled inlet waters averaged
19.5 mg chloride/L and the four outlet waters 12.5 mg/L, an observed difference
of 7.0 mg/L. Individual observations retain within-location spread. The supplied
design does not establish causation or a broader time/location population mean.”

**R4.** The exported values reproduce the conservation equation up to floating-
point rounding. Adsorption to a vessel, incomplete transfer or chemical loss
could break it; contaminated solvent could add analyte. A small computational
rounding tolerance is not an analytical acceptance criterion.
:::
